opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is a really important question, because a lot of our current measurement relies on comparing AIs to humans. We ask things like "can it do tasks that take a human expert an hour, or a day, or a month?" Once you're past the best human professionals, that anchor starts to break down, and you need some other way to talk about how much more capable systems are getting.

One frame I like is to think in terms of effective labor or effective compute. Instead of asking whether the AI can do a task at all, ask how much human-equivalent work it's producing. For example, if you have AIs automating AI research, how much faster is algorithmic progress going relative to a world with just the human researchers? You might say a given system is equivalent to having a thousand top researchers working at 10x speed, or whatever. That gives you a continuous quantity that keeps going up even after you've passed human level on any individual task.

A related idea is to measure the gap between successive AI generations directly, the way you might compare a median professional to the very best in a field. There's a pretty large spread in human ability: the best researchers in a field can be dramatically more productive than the median. So you can ask questions like: is the jump from this model to the next one comparable to going from a median ML engineer to a top-tier one? Is it like several of those jumps stacked on top of each other? I think that's a useful way of conveying how big qualitative capability gains are, even when you can't point to a human who sits at that level anymore.

You can also look at outcomes in the world. How quickly are hard open problems getting solved? How fast is the AI developing new technologies, or compressing what would have been years of R&D into months? Those are noisier, but they're ultimately what we care about.

And then there's a practical evaluation problem. Once AIs exceed us, it gets harder for humans to check their work. So you increasingly need tasks where verification is easier than generation, like formal math, or code with good tests, or predictions that resolve, or you need to use weaker trusted AIs to help evaluate stronger ones. That's tricky, and it's connected to the safety concerns, because the period when we can't easily evaluate what the systems are doing is also when misalignment or sandbagging would be hardest to detect.

So my overall view is: shift from "which human tasks can it do" toward "how much effective labor and speedup does it provide," complement that with comparisons to the spread of human skill, and invest a lot in evaluation methods that still work when the AI is smarter than the evaluators.

r001.rationale: The response says human comparisons stop providing a useful anchor and that another measure is needed, but it does not say we have particularly little grounding for interpreting progress above the human range.

r002.rationale: It compares model gains to differences across human skill levels, but does not suggest an IQ-like scale for characterizing capability beyond the best professionals.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key problem is that once you're past the top human professionals, your normal benchmarks stop working. Most of how we've measured AI progress so far is basically "how does it compare to humans on this task," and once it's better than any human on the task, the human comparison just doesn't give you a signal anymore. You've saturated the thing.

So the way I tend to think about it is less in terms of absolute capability and more in terms of what the AI is actually substituting for. One frame I like is: how much does it speed things up? If you have an AI that can do the work of your best researcher, the natural next question isn't "is it smarter than the researcher," it's "how many of them is it worth, and how fast do they run?" You can think about it as, okay, this is like having a hundred of my best people running at ten times speed, or a thousand at fifty times speed. That gives you a scale that keeps going after you pass the human frontier, because you're measuring in terms of effective labour rather than in terms of some test score.

And I think the thing people often miss is that a lot of the action is going to be in that parallelism and speed, not necessarily in the AI being qualitatively way beyond humans on any individual judgement. Like, early on, I'd expect systems that are roughly human-level on most of the relevant tasks, but you have an enormous number of copies and they're running much faster and they don't sleep and they can share context in ways humans can't. That's already a radically different regime even if no single instance is doing anything a smart human couldn't in principle do.

Then separately there's a question about qualitative capability, like, is it coming up with things that no human would come up with? And I think that's much harder to measure, and honestly I'm a bit sceptical of our ability to track it well in advance. The best proxies are probably things like: how much of the AI R&D loop is the AI doing itself, what's happening to the rate of algorithmic progress at the labs, are the humans in the loop becoming a bottleneck. If the people at the lab are mostly just approving things the AI proposes and they can't really evaluate them anymore, that's a pretty strong sign you're past the point where human-referenced metrics mean much.

So I'd say: measure in terms of effective workforce and speedup, watch the AI R&D feedback loop closely, and be humble about the fact that at some point you're measuring something you can't fully evaluate.

r001.rationale: The response says qualitative capability beyond human-level performance is much harder to measure, expresses skepticism about tracking it in advance, and recommends humility because it may become something we cannot fully evaluate.

r002.rationale: The response proposes measuring effective workforce and speedup, but does not suggest an IQ-like scale.

astra-6.text:
I think one important point is that the best human professionals aren’t a ceiling on how good you can be at these tasks. They’re just a reference point that’s particularly convenient for us to measure against. Once AI systems exceed that reference point, evaluation gets harder, but it doesn’t become impossible.

For example, in programming, you can ask whether a system can complete a larger project, whether the resulting software works, and how much time and money it takes. You don’t necessarily need a human who could have written the software themselves to check that it does what you wanted. Similarly, for scientific research, you can make predictions and run experiments. There’s an external check on whether you’re making progress.

I’d also distinguish being as good as the best human at a task from being able to do everything that human does over a long period. A system might give an excellent answer to a well-specified question but still struggle to choose which questions to work on, carry out a project over several months, or notice when its approach isn’t working. So there could be a lot of progress along those dimensions even after performance on shorter tasks looks superhuman.

Eventually, I think you’d want to look more at things like how much useful research these systems produce, or how quickly they can accomplish some substantial objective with a fixed budget. Those measurements are slower and messier than a benchmark score, but they’re closer to what we actually care about.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluation gets harder above the human reference point, but does not characterize interpreting further progress there as a question with particularly little grounding.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest using an IQ-like scale to characterize capability beyond the best human professionals.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one important thing is that matching the best human professionals isn’t a ceiling. You can ask how much faster the AI can do the work, how cheaply it can do it, and how many copies you can run. Even if each copy is only as good as a very good human, having a million of them working at ten times human speed could be a pretty enormous change.

But then there’s a harder measurement problem, which is: can they do things that the best humans can’t do? And there, you increasingly need to look at outcomes. Can they solve scientific problems that have been open for a long time? Can they develop better technology? In particular, can they make substantial improvements to AI systems themselves?

You don’t necessarily need a human who could have produced the answer to check whether it works. We can check a mathematical proof that we wouldn’t have come up with, or test whether a proposed engineering design performs better. But verification can be expensive, and sometimes it takes a long time. So I’d expect measuring progress to become more dependent on running substantial projects and seeing what actually happens, rather than just asking questions where we already have a good human answer.

r001.rationale: The response calls measuring abilities beyond the best humans a harder problem, but does not say we have particularly little grounding for assessing that progress.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest translating AI capability into an IQ-like scale.
